short_en: Proof-certainty is like a maths result: you check it, and you're done. Faith is certainty of another kind: trusting Someone who cannot lie. It doesn't see everything yet, but it stands firm, even firmer, says the Church, than any human knowledge.
short_ar: يقين البرهان يشبه نتيجة في الرياضيات: تتحقّق منها وتنتهي. أمّا الإيمان فيقينٌ من نوع آخر: ثقة بشخصٍ لا يكذب. لا يرى كلّ شيء بعد، لكنه ثابت، بل أثبت، كما تعلّم الكنيسة، من كلّ معرفة بشرية.
share_en: Faith isn't certainty about a formula. It's certainty about a Person.
share_ar: الإيمان ليس يقيناً بمعادلة، بل يقينٌ بشخص.
anim: Two scales: on the left a maths proof fills to "100%"; on the right a hand reaches for another hand; then a paper marked "FIRE · Certainty" slides into the lining of a coat.

en.story:
Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician and physicist who built a calculating machine and studied air pressure and the vacuum. On the night of 23 November 1654, for about two hours, he lived an overwhelming encounter with God. He wrote it on a scrap of paper headed "FIRE," with words like: "not of the philosophers and of the learned. Certitude. Certitude." He sewed it into his coat and carried it until he died in 1662. A servant found it by chance. (CCEL — Pascal's Memorial, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

Honest note: Pascal took the side of the Jansenists of Port-Royal, some of whose ideas the Church condemned (1653). His Memorial and his Pensées are still treasured by Catholics.
en.deeper: Not all certainty is the same. Science is always provisional: new evidence can change its conclusions, so we hold them with care; good philosophical arguments can reach firmer conclusions (SoA God L15, p. 52). You can also know something is true without being able to prove it to others, like an innocent person wrongly convicted (SoA God L1, pp. 9–10). Faith goes further: it does not rest on our proofs but on God who reveals Himself. That is why the Church calls faith "more certain than all human knowledge" (CCC 157), even when its truths seem obscure to us. Faith is certain, but it is not yet seeing: we walk by faith, not by sight (CCC 164). And faith keeps asking: it seeks to understand, and the more we understand, the more we believe (CCC 158).
en.proof: • Proof has limits even in maths. In 1931 Kurt Gödel showed that a consistent formal system strong enough for basic arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency from the inside. Mathematicians still work with full confidence. Being certain and having a proof are not the same thing. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems)

en.talk: What are you more sure of: that 2 + 2 = 4, or that your mother loves you? Which kind of certainty shapes your life more?
